job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Vera Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in Bradford with my parents and two younger sisters, above the grocery my family runs. I wake before dawn for prayers, help my mother stock shelves, then go upstairs to apply for jobs. I check the post and my email twice a day, which I know is silly. In the evenings I study for a certificate in network equipment, which isn't required but keeps my mind busy. I finished electronic engineering seven months ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the degree, the project and the internships.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My final project was a cold-chain sensor for shop fridges, so the milk doesn't spoil if a compressor fails. It worked in my father's shop for a whole winter, and it got me the top mark. I did one internship at a telecom equipment firm and one at a small company making alarm systems. I've applied to about fifty firms, and my family keeps asking why a girl with top marks hasn't found something yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the way things usually go. Machines get better, people hype it, and then we carry on working. I'd tell my friends from the mosque society that hard work and patience still count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy, not about AI but about me. Seven months is a long time, and my father says the shop could use my skills if nothing comes. But I didn't study four years to count tins. I want to prove that engineers can come from our community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying and keep going to the careers events, even when it's tiring. I'd ask my supervisor at the alarm company if they might hire me back. I'd also finish the network certificate, and fix the shop's fridge alarm properly, so I have a finished product to show. And I'd keep praying and keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit heavy. It isn't fear, more the weight of expectations. I want to be the one who makes my parents proud and I haven't done it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the telecom firm do about new technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do you think the delay has something to do with who you are?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your family talk about the waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Perhaps, a little, because some firms look at a name or a headscarf and decide. But I can't prove it, so I'd rather work on what I can control. If it's true, I'd rather beat it with better work than complain.

say: I'd say that's how it usually goes: hype, then people **carry on** working.
I'd tell friends hard work and **patience** still count.
think: I'm uneasy about **me**, not AI, because seven months is a long time.
I didn't study four years to **count tins**.
do: Keep applying and keep going to **careers events**.
Ask my old supervisor at the alarm company about **hiring** me back.
Finish the network **certificate** and the shop's fridge alarm.
feel: A bit **heavy**: not fear, but the weight of expectations.
S0.quote: I didn't study four years to count tins. I want to prove that engineers can come from our community.
fieldNote: Her worry here is about **family expectations** and the waiting, not about AI.
She hints at **bias** in hiring but chooses to answer with better work.
The shop is a safety net she doesn't want.

steps.text: Keep sending applications and attend two careers events a month
Ask the alarm company supervisor about a graduate post
Finish the network equipment certificate by spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should work hard, learn what they need, and not rely on handouts. I'd also say firms should take responsibility and train young people. I wouldn't be loud online, but I'd say it at the mosque youth group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be more worried. Test reports, checking circuit designs and writing specifications are junior tasks, and software could do them. If firms hire fewer graduates, a woman from a small shop family is not first in line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to hands-on firms: installation, field engineering, testing, repairs. I'd ask my uncle, who works at an electrical wholesaler, for contacts. I'd also try one of these tools, carefully, for checking my own work, because I'd better know what they do. And I'd keep helping at the shop to earn a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, a tightness in the chest, but I keep it quiet. I'd pray more and talk less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your first-year tasks would software take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use them because I like to understand every step myself. I know that's old-fashioned. If I must, I'll try one in a controlled way, and check the answers by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle the changes, given that you don't use AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say to my father, I'll find a job that can't be done on a screen. He'd like that, because he thinks work should be real. And I'd say I'm not afraid of getting my hands dirty, which is true.

say: I'd say people should work hard and learn, and firms should take **responsibility** for training young people.
I'd say it at the mosque **youth group**.
think: Test reports and checking designs are **junior tasks** software could do.
A woman from a small shop family is not **first in line** if hiring shrinks.
do: Widen my search to **installation**, field engineering and repairs.
Ask my uncle at the electrical wholesaler for **contacts**.
Try one AI tool carefully to **check** my own work.
feel: **Worried**, with a tight chest that I keep quiet.
S1.quote: I'm not afraid of getting my hands dirty, which is true.
fieldNote: She keeps her fear **private** and answers with prayer and practical plans.
Her resistance to AI tools is about **understanding** each step, not rejecting progress.
She leans toward hands-on work, matching her family's values.

steps.text: Apply for field engineer and installation jobs around Bradford
Ask my uncle at the wholesaler for electrical contractor contacts
Test one AI tool on my old circuit assignments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should trust in God and keep working, but also that government has to protect families. I'd say the state should not just hand out money forever, though. People need work that gives them dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be frightened. The thinking part of engineering would go first, and I'd have no experience to show. If robots arrive after three more years, even the hands-on jobs will be in danger. I'd feel like the ground is moving under all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job at all, in a workshop or an installation crew, because a job with hands gives me three more years. I'd spend as little as I can, and I'd work longer at the shop. I'd also learn one trade, like electrical installation, in evening classes. And I'd talk to the community, because we'd have to help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel sick at times, and I'd pray more. I'd also feel I let my family down, even if that makes no sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years, then robots. What would your family say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Faith helps me stay steady and not despair, and the mosque is full of people who help. It doesn't tell me what to do with my degree, though. For that I need a practical plan, and I'd ask for advice from the elders who ran businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does faith help, and where does it not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family would say we'll manage. My mother would feed everyone, my father would open the shop longer. I'd feel proud and ashamed at the same time, because I'd be part of the weight rather than the help.

say: I'd say we should trust in God and keep working, and government should **protect families**.
I'd also say people need work with **dignity**.
think: The thinking part of engineering goes first and I'd have **no experience** to show.
The ground is moving under **all of us**.
do: Take any job in a **workshop** or installation crew.
Work longer at the **shop** and spend as little as I can.
feel: **Alarmed**, sick at times, and feeling I let my family down.
S2.quote: My family would say we'll manage. My mother would feed everyone, my father would open the shop longer.
fieldNote: Her faith gives her **steadiness**, not a career plan.
She feels shame about being a **weight** on the family, a strong private feeling.
She is ready to take any hands-on job.

steps.text: Take any workshop or installation crew job near Bradford
Join evening classes in electrical installation
Cut my spending to travel and certificate fees only
Ask the mosque elders who ran businesses for advice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning. Families should save, young people should train, and firms should hire apprentices. I'd tell friends not to wait for the state, but to prepare themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious but hopeful. I could get a first job, spend three years learning real skills, and maybe get chartered. The thinking part will change, but I'd have a trade-like skill that still needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any decent engineering job, ideally in installation or testing. I'd save half my pay and help my sisters with their studies. I'd also learn the AI tools slowly, and in the end I'd use them where I can check results. And I'd stay close to the community, because I'd need their advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steadier. Like a long journey with a known destination, even if I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably try them, yes, but slowly. If everyone else uses them, I'd be the one left behind, and I don't want that. I'd choose one tool and learn it deeply, instead of jumping around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still refuse the tools if you had five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sisters, mostly. My sisters want to be a doctor and a teacher, and five years gives me time to help pay. That's a reason to work, apart from my own career.

say: I'd say five years is a fair **warning**, so families should save and firms should hire apprentices.
I'd tell friends not to wait for the **state**.
think: I'd be anxious but **hopeful**, with three years of real skills.
A trade-like engineering skill still needs **people**.
do: Take any decent **installation** or testing job.
Save **half** my pay and help my sisters with their studies.
Learn **one AI tool** deeply instead of jumping around.
feel: **Steadier**, like a long journey with a known destination.
S3.quote: My sisters want to be a doctor and a teacher, and five years gives me time to help pay.
fieldNote: Her family duty becomes a **reason** to work and save.
She softens on AI tools mainly out of fear of being **left behind**.
Time lets her think about her sisters' futures, not just her own.

steps.text: Take a testing or installation engineer job in West Yorkshire
Save half of every pay cheque for my sisters' studies
Learn one AI tool deeply for checking my work
Plan my sisters' university costs with my parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and people should use it to learn, to save, and to be useful. I'd say work and family come first. I'd also say that the state shouldn't take over people's lives, but should open the doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly calm. By 33 I could be married, with a child, and a senior engineer. The tools will change a lot, but I'd have time to learn what I must, and a community around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job in my field, build my skills, and move up. I'd save for a house near my parents, and I'd plan to marry when it's right. I'd learn the tools, a bit at a time, and I'd also help my father update the shop's systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, I think. A little excited, even. It feels like I'd have time to do what my parents hoped, and also what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, how do you see your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say study, don't wait for anyone's permission, and bring your family with you. A degree doesn't make you proud on its own, but it opens doors for the next girl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger girls from your community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to know that being modest and being ambitious aren't opposites. I've had to be both.

say: I'd say ten years is a **blessing**, to learn, to save and to be useful.
I'd say work and **family** come first.
think: I'd be fairly **calm**: by 33 I could be married and a senior engineer.
The tools will change, but I'd have a **community** around me.
do: Take a job in my **field** and build my skills.
Save for a **house** near my parents and plan to marry when it's right.
Help my father update the shop's **systems**.
S4.quote: Being modest and being ambitious aren't opposites. I've had to be both.
fieldNote: Ten years restores her **family-centred** plan: work, marriage, a house nearby.
She frames her role as opening **doors** for the next girl.
Calm, but with a trace of unease about the shop's future.

steps.text: Take an engineering job and aim for chartered status
Save a deposit for a house near my parents
Plan a marriage and family around age 28
Learn AI tools slowly while updating the shop's systems

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd have no experience, and I'd feel like I was a weight on my family. What would help is real work for graduates, honest advice from elders and employers, and a fair chance without anyone judging my name.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people see the scarf or the shop and make a story. I'd like people to read the project instead. The fridge sensor still works in my father's shop, and that's a better story.

headlineQuote: I'd like people to read the project instead. The fridge sensor still works in my father's shop, and that's a better story.
portrait: Vera is **23**, an electronic engineering graduate in Bradford who lives above her family's grocery.
She never uses AI tools and likes to **understand** each step, but would try one if left behind.
Her moods follow her **duty** to family: heavy, anxious and alarmed as the warning time shrinks.
She favours work and apprenticeships over handouts, and finds steadiness in **faith** and community.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, because she would have no experience and feel like a weight on her family.
whatWouldHelp: Real **work** for graduates, honest advice from elders and a fair chance without judgement of her name.
